title: Kestrel and the House
premise: Ulyana Marchetti, a folklorist and the last of the Marchetti line, returns to the family house in a mountain village to record the funeral songs locals refuse to sing twice. Their sleep recordings begin capturing a second voice that answers questions asked aloud, revealing the house keeps a count of its dead—and the well at the property's edge refills each time the count is settled. As Ulyana uncovers an ancestor's crime: a woman named Kestrel drowned in the well to secure the inheritance, they must choose between honoring their duty to preserve the family legacy and giving Kestrel justice outside any law. In the end, Ulyana renounces the inheritance, sings Kestrel's song twice themselves, and lets the house fall as the villagers carry them out ahead of the rising water.
about_author: Coral Marchetti is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing oral histories in remote European villages before turning to fiction. They write horror rooted in folklore, inheritance, and the things families agree never to say aloud.

chapters.title: The House That Counts
chapters.summary: Ulyana arrives at the decaying Marchetti house, ostensibly to record dying folk songs for an archive. The village greets them with polite dread; no one will meet their eyes. Exploring the house alone, Ulyana finds tally marks scratched inside every closet door. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: uneasy homecoming, the sense of being expected.

chapters.title: Songs Refused Twice
chapters.summary: In the village tavern, Ulyana asks an old woman, Baba Vesna, to sing the harvest lament. She begins, stops mid-verse, and refuses to repeat it, saying 'a song sung twice is an invitation.' Ulyana records the fragment anyway. That night, the house makes noises they explain away as pipes. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: professional curiosity curdling into unease.

chapters.title: Sleep Recordings
chapters.summary: A folklorist's habit: Ulyana leaves a recorder running overnight to capture ambient sound for archival context. Reviewing it, they hear footsteps pacing the hallway, a door opening that stays shut, and—most disturbing—their own sleeping voice asking questions they don't remember asking. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: rationalization under strain.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: The recordings now capture a second voice, low and wet-sounding, answering Ulyana's sleep-talk. It answers questions about the house, the family, the count. Ulyana plays the tape back awake and asks one question deliberately: 'Who are you?' The answer, hours later, while they slept: 'Kestrel.' POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: terror and strange tenderness intertwined.

chapters.title: What the Well Remembers
chapters.summary: Ulyana investigates the dry stone well behind the house, finding it oddly cold and faintly damp despite years of drought. At its lip, tally marks again—hundreds, going down into the dark. A villager watching from the fence warns them off without explanation. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: dread taking physical shape.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Ledgers
chapters.summary: In the attic, Ulyana finds household ledgers kept by three generations of Marchettis. Entries grow stranger: names crossed out, then added back, then annotated with dates of death that match the closet tallies. The last ledger, their grandmother's hand, ends mid-sentence. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: the horror of inheritance, evidence compounding.

chapters.title: Baba Vesna's Bargain
chapters.summary: Ulyana confronts Vesna, who finally explains: the house counts its dead, and the Marchettis have always paid it. Every generation, someone is given to the well so the rest may keep the land. The songs are laments for those payments—sung once, never twice, or the debt comes due. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: betrayal by one's own bloodline.

chapters.title: Kestrel's Verse
chapters.summary: Vesna, guilt-ridden, teaches Ulyana the forbidden second half of the harvest lament—a verse naming Kestrel, a servant girl the first Marchetti drowned in 1847 to claim her dowry and secure the estate. The song was composed by Kestrel herself before she died. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: grief for a stranger who feels like kin.

chapters.title: Questions in the Dark
chapters.summary: Ulyana begins speaking to Kestrel intentionally, leaving the recorder running and asking questions before sleep. Kestrel describes drowning slowly, watching the well refill around her, counting. She does not want vengeance, she says—she wants to be counted properly, sung home. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: love beginning where fear was.

chapters.title: The Cousins Arrive
chapters.summary: Word reaches distant Marchetti relatives that Ulyana is in residence; two cousins arrive uninvited, claiming the family must settle the estate before the matriarch's death anniversary. They know more than they admit and flinch at the well. The house's noises intensify with extra bodies under its roof. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: intrusion, competition, shared complicity.

chapters.title: Duty in the Ledger
chapters.summary: One cousin, Tomas, reveals the family's true errand: the count must be settled this year or the house will take what it's owed itself. He argues Ulyana, as the resident heir, owes the duty—a life for the land. Ulyana refuses, and that night the recordings capture Kestrel whispering warnings. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: love against duty, lines drawn.

chapters.title: Refill
chapters.summary: After a violent argument, the cousins attempt to force the matter; that night the dry well is found brimming with black water, though rain hasn't fallen. Something has begun collecting on its own. The village bars its doors. Ulyana realizes staying invisible was never an option—the house knows its heir. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: escalation, point of no return.

chapters.title: The Village That Paid
chapters.summary: Vesna confesses the village's full history: for generations they traded silence for safety, letting the Marchettis feed the well so the fields stayed fertile. Half the graveyard holds unnamed dead. The villagers will not help Ulyana—but some leave offerings at the fence. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: communal guilt, isolation deepening.

chapters.title: Tally
chapters.summary: Ulyana counts the marks in the closets against the ledgers and finds the numbers wrong: the house counts one more than the ledgers record, every generation. The extra mark, always, is Kestrel—never entered, never paid, never sung. The house has been waiting one hundred and seventy years. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: revelation, terrible clarity.

chapters.title: What Kestrel Wants
chapters.summary: In the deepest recording yet, Kestrel speaks clearly: she doesn't want a replacement body in the well. She wants her name in the ledger, her verse sung twice, and the inheritance returned to nothing—unclaimed, so no one ever owes the house again. Ulyana must renounce everything their name means. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: love demanding sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Cousins' Solution
chapters.summary: Tomas and his sister decide to solve the problem themselves: drug Ulyana and give them to the well, settling the count and inheriting clean. Ulyana wakes bound in the cellar as the water rises through the floor. Kestrel's voice fills the dark, furious. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: betrayal, near-drowning, desperation.

chapters.title: The Well Takes Its Own
chapters.summary: As the water climbs, Kestrel intervenes—not gently. The house turns on the cousins, the count recognizing their intent as payment offered. One cousin vanishes into the flooding cellar; Tomas flees into the night. Ulyana, freed, understands the house will not stop until the count is settled rightly. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: horror of rescue bought with another's life.

chapters.title: Sung Twice
chapters.summary: At dawn, Ulyana stands at the well's edge and sings Kestrel's lament complete—both halves, twice through, voice breaking but unceasing. With each repetition the water drops. Villagers gather at the fence, some weeping, some singing the response verses no archive ever recorded. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: catharsis, mourning made public at last.

chapters.title: Renunciation
chapters.summary: Ulyana writes the renunciation into the final ledger—every Marchetti name struck, the estate surrendered to no one—and enters Kestrel's name at last, dated 1847, marked 'counted.' The house goes silent, closets bare of marks. Kestrel's voice, one final time: thank you, and goodbye. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: grief and release braided together.

chapters.title: Before the Count
chapters.summary: The well begins to refill one last time, the house groaning as if exhaling a held breath. Vesna urges everyone out—'get the family out ahead of the count.' Ulyana carries the ledgers and recordings to high ground as the villagers help evacuate whatever can be saved. Tomas watches from the road, hollowed. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: urgency, exodus, acceptance.

chapters.title: The House Falls
chapters.summary: From the hillside, Ulyana watches the well overflow and the house sink into the ground it stood on for two centuries, swallowed without violence, like something finally allowed to rest. The village bells ring for the first time in living memory—for a funeral, not a warning. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: awe, exhaustion, peace.

chapters.title: Archive of the Unnamed
chapters.summary: Months later, Ulyana publishes the recordings and the completed song under Kestrel's name, not their own, donating the proceeds to the village. In the last scene, Ulyana plays the tapes one final time and hears only wind—then, faintly, a single hummed note, gone before it finishes. Some debts end; some just change hands. POV: Ulyana. Emotional beat: bittersweet closure, the past acknowledged but never fully silenced.
